abstract: Active sensing animals like echolocating bats and porpoises modulate their sensory volumes in a directed manner by altering various aspects (aim, beam width, source-level) of their calls or clicks, termed 'acoustic gaze'. Studying acoustic gaze requires inferring the beam parameters from a limited set of sensors, which is however a non-trivial task. To aid inference, studies apply a series of experimental constraints and data curation practices (e.g. animals always facing towards the array, only calls with peaks within X degrees of the centre analysed). Particularly for field studies, these constraints drastically reduce the volume of data, and remove important spatio-temporal context. Here I present a model-based Bayesian paradigm to perform acoustic gaze inference that releases the need for arbitrary constraints and curation practices such as animal flight direction or aim with three computational demonstrations 1) recovering acoustic gaze from a free-flying animal without constraints 2) post-hoc calibration of previously published array geometries that expand the spatial range of analysable calls and 3) a priori calibration of a proposed array design to avoid inefficient designs. The model-based paradigm expands the conditions under which acoustic gaze inference can be done, while also providing a principled approach to honestly estimate the uncertainty in estimated parameters.
